newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINLAND BANK SAYS MAY ACT FOR GOVERNMENT IN FOREX.
newsitem.headline: FINLAND BANK SAYS MAY ACT FOR GOVERNMENT IN FOREX.

text.p: The Bank of Finland may act on behalf of the government on the foreign exchange market, and such actions would not show in its balance sheet, a senior central bank official said on Wednesday.

"The central bank ensures that the government's need for currencies is satisfied, and that can be from the reserves or directly from the currency market," Markus Fogelholm, head of the market operations department, told Reuters.
This arrangement was started in January when the markka was under strong pressure to appreciate.
The government needs currencies to service its foreign debt.

Many operators expect the markka to rise against the German mark on strong economic fundamentals, and corporate treasury dealers said on Wednesday the Bank had been selling markka in London late on Tuesday when DEM/FIM inched below 2.70.
The markka and other Nordic currencies rose sharply on Wednesday to their highest levels against the German mark in three to four months.
Fogelholm declined to comment but said the bank can in principle make transactions with 60 banks in all, via brokers.

Bank of Finland board member Matti Vanhala said in February that the central bank's ambition is to keep the exchange rate close the central rate, and governor Sirkka Hamalainen said when the markka was linked to the ERM it was "quite clear that the definition of stability will not be plus-minus 15 (percent) ... and it is quite obvious that it is not 2-1/4 percent".
The 2.97 DEM/FIM rate broken on Tuesday is 2.36 percent below the central parity rate.

When the markka joined the ERM, the central bank said that if the markka's external value should come under pressure, the exchange rate would have to be defended even with stern measures, largely short-term interest rates, as currency intervention could only temporarily restrain pressures.
However, the bank warned in June that inflation risks had increased clearly: operators say a rate hike would boost the markka further.
